title: Women and Children on the Banks of a Stream
date: Date not given in the Met record
medium: Triptych of woodblock prints; ink and color on paper

altText: A wide Japanese woodblock print made of three joined sheets, showing women and children gathered together beside a stream.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record: title, artist, medium, culture, public-domain flag, credit line, tags (Human Figures, Children, Women) and image URLs read from the record; the record gives no object date

context: A triptych of color woodblock prints by Kitagawa Utamaro, a leading Japanese print designer of the Edo period. The Met record does not give a date, and its tags list human figures, children and women.

descriptions.k: Women and children are by a stream. There are three pictures side by side that make one big picture. Who do you see? What are the children doing? Where would you stand?
descriptions.g12: Utamaro made this print in Japan long ago. It has three parts that join into one wide picture. Women and children spend time beside a stream. Look at how the figures overlap and how their robes flow. Which group would you like to join? Why?
descriptions.g35: Kitagawa Utamaro was famous in Japan for prints of people in everyday life. This one is a triptych, which means three sheets that form one wide scene. It shows women and children beside a stream. Look at how the figures are grouped across the three parts. How does the artist keep your eye moving from one sheet to the next?
descriptions.g68: A triptych like this uses three woodblock-printed sheets to make a panoramic scene. Utamaro, known for his sensitive prints of women and family life, groups women and children by a stream so that the figures link across the sheet edges. The flowing robes and gestures carry the eye along. How does the wide format change the way we look compared with a single sheet, and what story does the grouping suggest?
descriptions.g910: Utamaro's triptych spreads a family-centered scene across three sheets, so the composition depends on rhythm and link rather than one central focus. Gestures, overlapping figures and flowing lines move the eye from sheet to sheet, while the stream anchors the setting. The Met record gives no date, so context must come from Utamaro's wider work. How do format, grouping and line shape the idea of community in this print?
descriptions.g1112: Utamaro's triptych is part of the Edo-period tradition of prints that idealized daily life. Its wide format invites a reading across sheets rather than a single focal point, and its attention to women and children has been interpreted both as affectionate observation and as a product shaped by the market for such images. Because the record gives no date, claims about its place in Utamaro's career need caution. How do format and subject support these competing readings?

teacherNote.context: Kitagawa Utamaro designed many Edo-period prints of women and family life. This triptych joins three sheets into one wide scene, and the Met record does not give a date.
directions: Have students cover two sheets and describe the scene, then uncover all three and compare.
Ask students to trace one flowing line across a sheet edge and explain how it links the sheets.
Compare this wide format with a single-sheet print and discuss what each lets the viewer see.
